newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Moevenpick growth tied to brand recognition.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Moevenpick growth tied to brand recognition.

text.p: Swiss hotel and restaurant group Moevenpick said on Tuesday it expected sales to resume growth this year and saw brand recognition and franchising, rather than direct investments, as the best sales strategy.

"We have seen too many firms which have expanded at the cost of their internal strength. That can be devastating," chief executive Ulrich Geissmann told journalists at the start of the annual news conference.
Moevenpick is well known in Switzerland and Germany, where its hotels and restaurants are run under its own name.
It also markets coffee, ice cream, smoked salmon and other luxury foods, sold under its brand.
Moevenpick's red and orange logo topped by a seagull is a ubiquitous trademark in its core Swiss and German markets, where the weak economy has hurt sales growth.
Total sales revenues fell slightly in 1996 to 1.112 billion francs ($757 million) from 1.116 billion in 1995, although group net profit rose to 22.4 million francs from 15.2 million.
"We believe that the sales shrinkage of 1996 has come to a halt," Moevenpick said in its annual report, adding: "As of the new business year (1997), we once again expect sales to grow."
Despite improved profitability, the restaurants division, responsible for about one-third of total revenues, saw turnover fall 10 percent to 368 million francs in 1996 from 1995's 409 million.
Half of that drop was attributed to the sale of some activities but the other half, according to Geissmann, was due to "genuine declines in revenues".
Part of the problem is a weak business climate in Europe.
Switzerland, in its seventh year of depressed growth, accounts for roughly half of Moevenpick's turnover.
Swiss revenues fell 4.3 percent in 1996 to 551 million francs from 576 million in 1995. Revenues from Germany also fell to 346 million, down 4.7 percent from 363 million in 1995.
Geissmann called 1996 a "year of new openings" but mainly in Europe. For 1997, Moevenpick will emphasise expansion beyond Europe.
Part of the trick will be to continue to expand despite dependence on weak home markets.
Its strategy includes focusing on a few "reproducible concepts", Geissmann said, calling for a "deliberate strengthening of corporate identity."

Geissmann said the company would make new inroads beyond Europe in future, especially in Asia and the Mideast. It has signed an agreement to open a total of 55 new restaurants under franchises in those areas, as well as new hotels.

Moevenpick plans to raise its dividend on 1996 results to seven francs per bearer share and per participation certificate from six for 1995. The dividend per registered share was raised to 1.40 francs from 1.20.
Paul Schwizer, general director for finance and controlling, said the company remained optimistic for 1997 after both revenues and profits grew in the first quarter.

"We can report gains in revenues as well as profit, in fact good gains," said Schwizer, adding revenues rose by five percent in the first three months. He said company policy was to increase the dividend when profits rose.

The outcome in 1997 was likely to depend in part on the strength of the Swiss franc, a continued weakening of which would be seen as positive for overall results. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340 ($ = 1.468 Swiss Francs)
